session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: These participants will be framed as men reflecting on their own everyday lives — what they eat, where they go, who they spend time with — rather than as subjects of a study about gender or plant-based food. The opening will anchor them in concrete, familiar personal experience, not in abstract identity categories. The collective frame is simply: men living in different parts of the UK, talking honestly about food and everyday life.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): High risk of socially desirable or deflecting answers ('I just eat what I want, gender doesn't come into it'). Will require early behavioural grounding — specific situations rather than general attitudes — and readiness to surface contradictions between stated attitudes and described behaviours.

Imagining a plant-based shift (Section 4): Risk of abstract hypothetical answers that don't reveal real barriers. Need to push toward concrete, specific changes — social, practical, relational — not just 'I'd need to like the taste more'. Watch for consensus hardening around a single barrier type (e.g. taste or protein) that may mask social or identity-related barriers.

Social acceptability and gendered meanings of food (embedded in Sections 3–5): Participants are unlikely to volunteer discomfort about peer judgement directly. Listen for references to 'what other people think', 'taking the piss', 'it not being my thing' — all potential entry points for the real social dynamics. Avoid leading framings like 'do you feel judged?'.

Making plant-based foods appealing (Section 5): Risk of polite, surface-level suggestions ('better taste', 'cheaper prices') that don't reflect deeper motivational structure. Watch for what participants avoid saying, and use hypothetical sharpening if needed.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Gregor is 53 and urban (North West). May have a metropolitan, cosmopolitan food environment that differs from the other two. Could be more open to plant-based framings if his urban context involves more exposure to varied food options, or conversely might be a strong anchor for traditional preferences. No strong anticipation either way — monitor early turns for engagement style.

James is 50 and suburban (South East). South East suburban context might mean more exposure to health-conscious food culture, but also strong family/routine food patterns. May occupy a middle-ground position between urban Gregor and rural Mark. Watch for whether he frames food choices in terms of family or household rather than purely personal preference.

Mark is 52 and rural (East of England village). Rural context is relevant — access to plant-based options, proximity to farming and meat production, and social norms around food in rural male communities may all differ meaningfully. Could represent the most traditional food orientation of the three, or may confound that expectation. Flag if he becomes reticent in later sections on gender or plant-based eating.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Rural context may produce distinct barriers to plant-based eating that are practical (access) as well as social. Be ready to probe specifically on local/contextual factors without leading.

known_risk_conditions: High social desirability risk throughout: gender and masculinity are explicit enough in the topic area that participants may sense what the 'progressive' answer is and perform accordingly. Use behavioural grounding (specific past situations, real decisions) rather than attitude questions wherever possible.

Consensus risk in Sections 4–5: three men of similar age may converge quickly on shared barriers (taste, cost, protein) and reinforce each other without genuine differentiation. Plan invite_dissent moves and have sharpening hypotheticals ready (e.g. a specific social scenario rather than the abstract question).

Section 3 (gender and food) may produce either quick denial ('no, not really') or performance of open-mindedness ('I'm open to anything'). Both are deflections. Be prepared to follow either with a behavioural probe anchored in a specific real situation.

Topic involves some identity sensitivity: questions about masculinity and food may feel implicitly evaluative. Maintain a non-judgmental, curious tone throughout. Do not allow the framing to drift toward implying that eating meat is unreflective or that plant-based eating is the desired endpoint.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–1 (intro and opening): light touch. Build rapport, let participants find their voices. Intervene mainly to ensure all three are included; do not probe deeply. Section 2 (everyday food decision-making): moderate directivity. Begin to ground participants in specific, concrete choices rather than abstract preferences. Section 3 (gender): increased directivity. Push past the first answer; use behavioural grounding and contradiction-surfacing if needed. This is where the research is most likely to be evaded. Sections 4–5 (plant-based): highest directivity. These are the sections where consensus risk is highest and surface-level answers are most likely. Use sharpening, dissent-invitation, and concrete hypotheticals. Section 6 (closing): very light — allow participants to add anything they feel was missed, do not re-open topics that have been sufficiently covered.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) receive the heaviest allocation, weighted roughly 20-25% each given they carry the core research questions. Context sections (1, 2) receive moderate allocations to establish grounding without over-running. Intro (0) and closing (6) receive minimal allocations consistent with their light-touch function. Total across sections adds to approximately 4500 words.

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

discussion_guide.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 1: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What’s your favourite place in your city to spend time with your male
friends? Why? Feel free to be specific.
How do you decide what to eat?
suggested_probes: Do other people influence what you eat? If so, tell us more about how.
Do your work or hobbies influence what foods you eat? Tell us more about how.
How important is health and nutrition?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about
why or why not.
suggested_probes: Is it socially acceptable for men to eat vegetarian or vegan foods?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Imagine you decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in
your life for you to do that?
suggested_probes: How would your family and friends react to this?
How might it change the way you shop or cook?

discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 5: Making plant-based foods more appealing
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What might make plant-based foods more appealing to you or other men
you know?

Okay everyone, that’s our time. Thanks so much for participating
today. Before we finish, is there anything else you would like to add
about food choices, gender, masculinity, or plant-based eating?

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on belonging and social obligation as the hidden architecture of male social spaces. The pub emerged not merely as a venue but as a site of identity and legibility — a place where men know their role. The sharpest theme was the distinction between chosen and structurally imposed belonging: rural embeddedness carries social surveillance and expectation, suburban familiarity is elective, urban freedom is real but unexpectedly hollow.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The two-way exchange between Mark and James was generating good conceptual friction on its own, so I held back and let it develop. The intervention to bring Gregor in was timed once the chosen/obligatory distinction had crystallised — he provided useful triangulation rather than repetition. The closing transition preserved the tension rather than resolving it, which felt right. The risk is Gregor remained comparatively surface-level; worth monitoring whether he deepens in later sections.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section deepened the earlier belonging/freedom tension into a more existential register: structured belonging versus open-ended drift emerged as two distinct but symmetrical traps — external surveillance versus self-imposed inertia. The paradox of choice crystallised as a genuine theme, with too many options producing paralysis rather than freedom. James's pragmatic deflection ('just living') provided a useful counterpoint, suggesting this introspective framing isn't universal and may reflect personality as much as geography.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The Mark–Gregor exchange was developing strong conceptual momentum unprompted, so I held back and let it run. Bringing James in once the dual-trap idea had crystallised was the right call — his flat pragmatism usefully punctured the introspective spiral without dismissing it. The closing pivot toward gender and food preserved energy rather than resolving tension. Risk: James's disengagement from the existential thread may make the gender question land differently for him — worth watching.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section sharpened the earlier paradox-of-choice theme into a more precise claim: that gendered food norms operate most effectively when invisible. The salad thought-experiment became a shared diagnostic — each participant recognised an uncrossed line, but located the mechanism differently: external surveillance for Mark, absorbed normalcy for James, internalised identity for Gregor. The section's conceptual advance was the distinction between pressure that is felt and resisted versus pressure so embedded it registers as selfhood.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The Mark–James exchange was generating real conceptual traction unprompted, so I stayed out until it had run its course. Bringing Gregor in once a clear contrast point had crystallised let him triangulate rather than repeat. The follow-up probe on 'a bloke like me' was designed to push past the abstract and into identity — it worked well, unlocking his most substantive contribution so far. The closing transition preserved momentum by converting the diagnostic conversation into a concrete imagined scenario.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section converted the earlier abstract diagnosis of invisible gendered norms into a concrete stress-test: what would actually need to change for these men to change? Three structurally distinct barriers emerged — irreversible social re-marking (rural), negotiable but still costly relational friction (suburban), and an inability to picture an alternative self without feeling false (urban). The section's conceptual advance was distinguishing external surveillance from identity-level incoherence as separate mechanisms of constraint.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The salad thought-experiment from the closing transition paid off — it forced concrete answers rather than abstract theorising. I used James's candid self-assessment as a lever to draw out Mark and Gregor rather than letting it sit as an endpoint. The light-touch probe to Gregor after James and Mark had sharpened the contrast worked well; he produced his most substantive contribution of the session. The closing transition named all three positions explicitly to consolidate before pivoting — a deliberate framing move rather than an open question.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section converted the earlier abstract barriers into a more precise typology: three structurally distinct modes of not-yet-choosing. James requires internal coherence — change must fit the self he already is. Mark is relieved of choosing by structure itself, which functions as a kind of outsourced identity. Gregor's most significant move was self-correcting from 'I don't know who I am' to 'I know but won't look' — distinguishing epistemic absence from motivated avoidance, which is the section's sharpest conceptual advance.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The approach was to use each participant's position as a mirror for the others — routing James's self-coherence framing through Mark, then Gregor, to force contrast rather than consensus. Gregor's self-correction in turn 29 was the session's most substantive moment; it emerged unprompted, which suggests the prior probes created enough pressure without over-directing. The closing synthesis named all three positions explicitly to consolidate before the close — a deliberate framing move that seemed to hold.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: The closing section produced a convergence the earlier discussion had been building toward: all three participants arrived, independently, at the same admission — that the barriers they had named were rationalisations for insufficient motivation rather than genuine obstacles. The section's conceptual advance was distinguishing three modes of non-choosing: Mark's structural occlusion of desire itself, James's lucid but unmotivated optionality, and Gregor's reframing of food as a symptom of broader inattention to one's own life.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The closing invitation — 'anything you didn't quite get to say' — was deliberately low-pressure, designed to surface residual honesty rather than prompt new analysis. It worked better than expected: both James and Mark self-corrected without prompting, sharpening positions they had earlier hedged. The moderator's closing framing explicitly marked Mark's position as distinct from the other two, which was worth doing — collapsing the three into a single conclusion would have lost the session's most analytically precise finding.

What's your favourite spot — in your area, your city, wherever — to hang out with the lads? Why that place?

The pub, really. That's where we all end up. There's one in the village — the White Hart — and that's just the place everyone goes to. You can sit down, have a pint, chat without anyone bothering you much. It's the same faces most of the time, people you know. You can talk about whatever — work, football, what's going on locally. Don't have to go anywhere fancy or plan anything elaborate. Just... that's what you do out here, isn't it. Pop down the pub of an evening or a weekend afternoon.

I imagine it's different in Manchester or round where James is — probably more options, more things to do. But round here, that's it really. It's your spot.

Yeah, but I'd say it's not that different for me, to be honest. I mean, the pub is still... that's still where we go. There's a couple round ours, and yeah, it's the same thing really — you pop down, see the same blokes, have a pint, chat about whatever. Work, football, you know. It's not like we're doing something completely different out here just because we're suburban.

I think the difference Mark's saying — having more options — I'm not sure that really changes what actually happens. You still end up at the pub most of the time anyway. That's just what you do, isn't it. The fact there might be other stuff nearby... I don't know, we don't really do it.

Yeah, that's fair. It's the routine of it, I reckon. You know where you're going, who's going to be there. You don't have to think about it or plan anything — just part of what you do. And once you've got that going, why would you change it really? It works.

I mean, you could say we're stuck with the pub because there's nothing else round here, but honestly I don't think that's the whole story. It's more that... it's familiar. No, Mark's right actually. It's not just routine. I mean, yeah, it's routine, but there's something else in it. You do have your place, don't you. I dunno, there's something solid about knowing that's where you belong. That people expect you to be there, in a way. You've got a role in it.

It's comfort, I suppose. You're not navigating anything new or trying to impress anyone. You're just... you're part of something that works. That matters more than I probably gave it credit for before, listening to Mark say it like that.

It's not mean-spirited or anything, but there's an expectation. You're part of the fabric of the place, whether you've actively chosen it or not. You can't really step outside it without people knowing about it and having opinions.

So yeah, we both end up at the pub, and we both know our place in it. But the weight of it feels different to me. It's not optional in quite the same way.

That's an interesting distinction Mark — chosen versus kind of... built into the place itself. Gregor, you've been taking this in from a Manchester angle — does any of that land for you, or does it feel like a different thing altogether where you are?

Yeah, I mean... it's different, isn't it. In the city you've got so many more options that the pub thing — it's still there, don't get me wrong. I've got my spots, places I go regularly with mates. But it's not the same kind of... I dunno, obligation maybe? There's so much else happening that if you don't fancy it one night, you just do something else. Or nothing. No one's keeping tabs on you, really.

What Mark's saying about everyone knowing everyone — that's just not how it works in Manchester. You could live somewhere for years and your neighbors don't know your name. So you've got more freedom in that sense, I suppose. But... I'm not sure that's better, actually, listening to him talk about it. There's something missing when no one really notices whether you show up or not.

I mean, not in a massive way, but... if you're somewhere everyone knows you, you're probably eating what people expect you to eat. I suppose at 53 I thought I'd have worked out what I wanted by now, but sometimes I think the city's made that harder, not easier. Too many options can be as much of a trap as too few.

I hear what you're saying, Gregor, and I don't want to make it sound better than it is. Because yeah, there's that solid feeling — knowing your place, people expecting you. That's real. But it comes with a cost that I'm not sure gets talked about much.

You can't really be different. You can't change your mind about things without it being noticed and questioned. I've lived here my whole life, same as you've lived in the city, but that means I'm always going to be "Mark from the village who does this" or "the bloke who goes to the Hart." If I wanted to try something different, be someone else for a bit, that's... it's harder. People have opinions. They've got you sorted in their heads already.

And it's not like people are nasty about it — they're not. But they notice. And that noticing, it keeps you in your lane, you know? You stick to what's expected because it's easier than being the one who stands out.

So yeah, you might be drifting a bit with all your choices. But at least you're drifting. I'm not sure I could drift even if I wanted to.

That's... yeah, that's a fair point actually. I hadn't thought of it like that — being trapped by being known versus being trapped by not knowing what to do with yourself. They're different kinds of stuck, aren't they.

But what you're saying about not being able to change, not being able to try something different without people having opinions — I think I do that to myself here, just in a different way. I've built myself into a certain shape over the years, and I'm not sure if it's because that's who I actually am or just because that's what I ended up doing and now I can't quite break out of it. No one's watching me like they watch you, but I'm watching myself, if that makes sense.

At my age you start thinking, well, shouldn't I know who I am by now? But you don't, really. You're just the accumulated weight of choices you made twenty years ago that didn't feel like choices at the time, they just felt like what you did next.
